q: Crossing the Saronic Gulf at midday, the whole crew wants to eat lunch below. What does Rule 5 require?
a: Someone keeps a lookout on deck at all times
o: The autopilot alarm is enough in daylight
A quick look round every 15 minutes will do
A lookout is only required at night
why: Rule 5: a proper lookout by sight and hearing at all times.

fig.title: Midday passage
lines: Ferries and fast boats on the route

q: How do you keep a proper lookout, sailing like this?
a: Look under the genoa to leeward regularly
o: Watch ahead and to windward only
Leave it to others — they can see you
Rely on the AIS alarm to warn you
why: Rule 5: the genoa hides the leeward bow — that is where you must look.

q: You are approaching this harbour at night. What does the scene mean for your speed?
a: Slow down — shore lights hide other vessels
o: Keep speed to clear the entrance quickly
Speed only matters in poor visibility
Keep to the harbour limit, nothing more
why: Rule 6: background light is a factor in choosing a safe speed.

fig.note: Night · harbour entrance against the town lights

q: Fog comes down while you are motoring along the Croatian coast. What speed do you choose?
a: Slow enough to stop well within 200 m
o: Full speed to get out of it sooner
Exactly half your usual cruising speed
Any speed — others must avoid you
why: Rules 6 and 19: a safe speed lets you stop within the distance you can see.

q: You are entering this harbour under power. How fast do you go?
a: Slowly — traffic density sets a safe speed
o: Cruising speed — the visibility is good
Fast, to spend less time in everyone's way
Any speed you like — others will avoid you
why: Rule 6: the density of traffic is a key factor in safe speed.

q: You are motoring in fog with this radar picture. What does Rule 6 say about relying on it?
a: Small boats may hide in the clutter — go slower
o: Nothing is there — keep your speed
Turn up the gain until the clutter clears
With radar on you may keep cruising speed
why: Rule 6(b): radar limits, sea state and clutter count in choosing a safe speed.

fig.title: Fog, short steep sea
lines: Radar: sea clutter out to 0.5 M

q: How do you keep a proper lookout by hearing in these conditions?
a: Post someone forward and stop now and then to listen
o: Keep the engine loud so that others can hear you
Listen from the cockpit, right beside the engine
Hearing does not count — only sight matters
why: Rule 5: lookout by sight and hearing — get away from the engine noise.

q: You take three hand-bearing compass bearings of a ship. What do they tell you?
a: Risk of collision exists
o: She will pass ahead of you
She will pass astern of you
No risk — the bearing moved 1°
why: Rule 7: a steady compass bearing with the range closing means risk of collision.

q: You take these bearings of a ship on your port bow. What will she do?
a: Pass astern of you — the bearing is drawing aft
o: Pass ahead of you — the bearing is drawing forward
Hit you — the bearing is steady
Cross ahead — she is on your port bow
why: Rule 7: a bearing drawing aft means she will pass astern; keep checking.

q: The bearing of this cruise ship is changing. Can you relax?
a: No — so close to a big ship, risk may still exist
o: Yes — any change of bearing means there is no risk
Yes — a ship that size is bound to have seen you
Only once the bearing has moved by 10° or more
why: Rule 7(d)(ii): risk can exist with a changing bearing when close to a large vessel.

q: What does Rule 7 say about this radar echo?
a: Plot it over time before deciding it will pass
o: It is far off — ignore it until it is seen
Assume it is a buoy until it moves
Turn to port now to open the range
why: Rule 7(c): no assumptions on scanty information, especially radar.

fig.title: Radar, haze at dusk
lines: One echo at 4 M on the starboard bow

q: You cannot tell whether the bearing of this motorboat is changing. What do you assume?
a: That risk of collision exists
o: That she will pass clear
That she has seen you
Nothing until you are sure
why: Rule 7(a): if in doubt, risk of collision is deemed to exist.

fig.note: Bearing hard to read in the swell

q: Your plotter shows this AIS target. What do you make of it?
a: Risk of collision — plan early action now
o: No risk — 0.1 M is a clear pass
Wait until she is in sight to decide
She has AIS, so she has seen you
why: Rules 7 and 8: a CPA near zero means risk of collision; act early.

fig.title: AIS target
lines: Not yet in sight in the haze

q: Can you rely on the AIS screen for your lookout here?
a: No — many boats carry no AIS at all
o: Yes — every vessel must carry AIS
Yes, for anything inside 10 M
Yes, as long as it is daylight
why: Rules 5 and 7: AIS is only an aid; yachts and fishing boats often have none.

fig.title: Haze, visibility 1 mile
lines: AIS screen: no targets within 10 M
Radar: switched off to save power
Fishing boats often work this coast

q: You must give way to this ship. What kind of alteration does Rule 8 want?
a: One early turn, big enough to see on radar
o: Several small 5° nudges as she closes
A late turn once she is close
A small change of speed only
why: Rule 8: early, substantial, readily apparent — not a series of small alterations.

q: You are the give-way vessel but cannot turn to starboard. What do you do?
a: Slow down or stop and let her pass ahead
o: Turn to port and cross ahead of her
Hold course and speed — you have no choice
Speed up to get across her bow
why: Rules 8(e) and 16: slowing or stopping is a proper give-way action.

fig.note: Shoal water close on your starboard side

q: You have turned 40° to starboard to pass astern of this boat. What does Rule 8 require now?
a: Check her bearing until she is past and clear
o: Return to your original course at once
Nothing more — the turn itself was enough
Sound one short blast every minute until clear
why: Rule 8(d): check the action until the other vessel is finally past and clear.

q: Under sail in this channel, risk of collision with the tanker now exists. Does your duty change?
a: No — you must still act early not to impede her
o: Yes — you become stand-on and hold course
Yes — the duty ends once she is close
No — but only if she sounds five short
why: Rule 8(f): the duty not to impede continues when risk of collision develops.

fig.note: Narrow channel · she can only use the deep water

q: You want to cross this buoyed channel ahead of the ship. What does Rule 9 say?
a: Do not cross if it will impede her — wait
o: Cross now — she must give way to you
Cross at speed — she can slow down
Cross diagonally to save time
why: Rule 9(d): do not cross a narrow channel if it impedes a vessel confined to it.

fig.note: Narrow channel · she can only use the channel

q: You are motoring up a winding channel and nearing a bend where high ground hides what is coming. What sound signal do you give?
a: One prolonged blast
o: Five short blasts
Two prolonged blasts
One short blast
why: Rule 34(e): one prolonged blast when nearing a bend that may hide other vessels.

q: Close to a blind bend in a narrow channel, you hear a prolonged blast from behind the headland. What do you do?
a: Reply with one prolonged blast and keep right
o: Reply with five short blasts
Stay silent and speed up round the bend
Reply with one short blast and cut the corner
why: Rule 34(e): a prolonged blast from round the bend is answered with one prolonged.

q: In this narrow channel you want to overtake on her port side. What do you sound first?
a: Two prolonged then two short blasts
o: Two prolonged then one short blast
Two short blasts
Long, short, long, short
why: Rule 34(c): two prolonged + two short = I intend to overtake on your port side.

fig.note: Narrow channel · you are the faster boat

q: After your overtaking signal in a channel, the boat ahead replies like this. What does it mean?
a: She agrees — overtake with care
o: She objects — stay astern
She is altering to starboard
She is going astern
why: Rule 34(c)(ii): prolonged, short, prolonged, short = agreement.

q: In a narrow channel you signal that you want to overtake. The boat ahead answers with five short blasts. What now?
a: Stay astern until it is safe and she agrees
o: Overtake at once — she has heard your signal
Overtake her on the other side instead
Sound five short back, then overtake
why: Rule 34(d): five short = doubt; do not overtake yet.

q: In a narrow channel this motor vessel astern sounds two prolonged and two short blasts. What do you do?
a: Sound agreement and move over to starboard
o: Move to port and hold your speed
Speed up so she cannot pass
Nothing — she must keep clear of you
why: Rule 9(e): if you agree, answer long-short-long-short and make room.

fig.note: Narrow channel · she is closing from astern

q: You must cross this traffic separation scheme. How do you steer?
a: On a heading at right angles, whatever the stream
o: On a track at right angles, heading into the stream
At a shallow angle, going with the traffic flow
Straight across towards your destination
why: Rule 10(c): cross on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the flow.

q: You want to follow the eastbound lane along the coast. How do you join it?
a: At its end, or from the side at a small angle
o: From the side, at right angles to the lane
Straight across the separation zone into it
Anywhere along it, in either direction
why: Rule 10(b)(iii): join at the end, or from the side at as small an angle as practicable.

q: Your 13 m yacht is going from one bay to the next along this coast. May you use the inshore traffic zone?
a: Yes — under 20 m and sailing vessels may
o: No — it is for fishing vessels only
Only with permission from VTS
No — you must use the lane
why: Rule 10(d): vessels under 20 m, sailing vessels and fishing vessels may use it.

q: Your planned track runs straight down the middle of the separation zone. Is that acceptable?
a: No — enter it only to cross or in an emergency
o: Yes — it is the safe space between the ships
Yes, provided you show a cone by day
Yes, but only in good daylight visibility
why: Rule 10(e): keep out of a separation zone except to cross, join, leave or in an emergency.

q: You are in this lane of a traffic separation scheme. What is wrong?
a: You are going against the traffic flow
o: Nothing — lanes are two-way for yachts
You should be in the separation zone
Nothing, if you keep to the edge
why: Rule 10(b)(i): in a lane, go in the general direction of traffic flow.

q: Your route passes close to where this scheme ends. What do you expect there?
a: Ships changing course and converging
o: No traffic — ships have left the lanes
Ships slowing down to anchor
Ships giving way to yachts there
why: Rule 10(f): navigate with particular caution near the ends of a scheme.

q: Crossing the lane under sail, this ship following the lane is closing on a steady bearing. Who keeps clear?
a: You — you must not impede a ship in the lane
o: The ship — power always gives way to sail
Nobody — both hold course inside the scheme
The ship — you are crossing at right angles
why: Rule 10(j): sail and vessels under 20 m must not impede power vessels in a lane.

fig.note: Crossing a TSS lane under sail

q: To cross this scheme at right angles under sail you would be head to wind. What do you do?
a: Motor-sail to hold a heading near right angles
o: Tack across at whatever angle the wind allows
Sail along the lane until the wind frees
Cross on a diagonal — ships give way to sail
why: Rule 10(c): cross as nearly at right angles as practicable — use the engine.

q: This yacht to windward is running downwind and you cannot see her mainsail. Who keeps clear?
a: You — you cannot be sure of her tack
o: She does — she is to windward
She does — she is running free
Neither, until you know her tack
why: Rule 12(a)(iii): on port tack, if unsure of a windward boat's tack, keep clear.

fig.note: Her mainsail is hidden behind the genoa

q: Both yachts are close-hauled on port tack and converging. What do you do?
a: Hold course and speed — she is to windward
o: Bear away — you are the leeward boat
Tack at once onto starboard
Give way — she is on your port side
why: Rule 12(a)(ii): on the same tack, windward keeps clear; you stand on (Rule 17).

q: You are to windward of this yacht. Who gives way?
a: She does — she is on port tack
o: You do — you are to windward
You do — she is close-hauled
Whichever boat is faster
why: Rule 12(a)(i): on different tacks, port keeps clear; windward only counts on the same tack.

q: You are running dead downwind with the mainsail out to port. This yacht is converging. Who keeps clear?
a: She does — you count as starboard tack
o: You do — running, you have no tack
You do — she is on your starboard side
Neither — pass each other port to port
why: Rule 12(b): the windward side is opposite the mainsail, so main to port = starboard tack.

q: You are stand-on to this port-tack yacht a mile away. Your crew want to tack away now, just in case. What do you do?
a: Hold course and speed so she can keep clear
o: Tack now so as to be on the safe side
Bear away now to pass astern of her
Luff up and slow right down for her
why: Rule 17(a)(i): the stand-on vessel keeps her course and speed.

q: This motor yacht is coming up from here, faster than you. Who keeps clear?
a: She does — she is overtaking you
o: You do — she is on your starboard side
Both alter course to starboard
You do — she is the faster boat
why: Rule 13: from more than 22.5° abaft your beam she is overtaking, whatever the side.

fig.note: She is closing from your starboard quarter

q: You are catching this motorboat up and cannot be sure whether you are overtaking or crossing. What do you do?
a: Assume you are overtaking and keep clear
o: Treat it as crossing: she gives way to you
Hold course and speed until it is clear
Pass close ahead of her as stand-on
why: Rule 13(c): in doubt, assume you are overtaking and keep out of the way.

fig.note: You are faster · about 20° abaft her beam

q: You started overtaking this boat from astern; now she is converging with you. Who keeps clear?
a: You — until you are past and clear
o: She does — she is now crossing from port
Neither — you are now abreast
She does — she is the slower boat
why: Rule 13(d): a later change of bearing does not end the overtaking vessel's duty.

fig.note: Bearing now forward of your beam

q: Motoring at night, this is the only light ahead and you are gaining on it. What do you do?
a: Keep clear — you are coming up from astern
o: Hold course — it must get out of your way
Pass close down either side at speed
Stand on and flash your spotlight
why: Rule 13: seeing only her sternlight, you are overtaking and keep clear.

q: Sailing downwind, you are catching up this yacht. Who keeps clear?
a: You — overtaking beats the tack rules
o: She does — she is on port tack
She does — she is to leeward
Neither — both boats are running
why: Rule 13 overrides Rule 12: an overtaking sailing vessel keeps clear.

q: Under sail, you see this motor yacht coming up from astern. What do you do?
a: Hold course and speed — she keeps clear
o: Alter course to let her pass
Slow down so she passes quickly
Give way — she is the faster vessel
why: Rules 13 and 17: she is overtaking and keeps clear; you stand on.

fig.note: She is faster, closing from astern

q: Looking astern at night, you see these lights closing on you. What do you do?
a: Hold course and speed and watch her
o: Turn to starboard as for head-on
Turn to port to let her pass
Speed up to stay ahead of her
why: Rules 13 and 17: a vessel coming up from astern is overtaking; you stand on.

fig.note: Night · dead astern of you, closing fast

q: Motoring at night, these lights appear fine ahead on a steady bearing. What do you do?
a: Alter course to starboard
o: Alter course to port
Hold course and speed
Stop and wait for her to act
why: Rule 14: masthead lights in line and both sidelights = head-on; both turn to starboard.

q: Motoring, you meet this yacht under sail end-on. Who takes action?
a: You alone — power keeps clear of sail
o: Both of you — each turns to starboard
She does — sail is more agile than power
Neither — you pass port to port as you are
why: Rule 14 is for two power vessels; Rule 18 makes power keep clear of sail.

q: This vessel is nearly ahead and her red light comes and goes. What do you do?
a: Treat it as head-on and alter to starboard
o: Alter to port to open the gap
Hold on for a starboard-to-starboard pass
Wait until both sidelights are steady
why: Rule 14(c): if in doubt whether it is head-on, assume it is and act.

fig.note: Night · fine on your starboard bow, closing

q: Motoring by day, you see this ship ahead with her masts in line. What do you do?
a: Alter course to starboard
o: Alter course to port
Hold your course and speed
Stop and wait for her
why: Rule 14: masts in line by day = head-on; both turn to starboard.

q: Motoring, you see this boat crossing. What do you do?
a: Hold course and speed, and watch her
o: Turn to port to pass astern of her
Slow down to let her cross ahead
Turn to starboard to give way
why: Rules 15 and 17: you are on her starboard side, so you stand on.

q: In open water, this high-speed ferry is closing on a steady bearing. Who gives way?
a: The ferry — you are on her starboard side
o: You — high-speed craft have priority
You — the bigger vessel has right of way
Both of you alter to starboard
why: Rule 15: a high-speed craft is a power-driven vessel with no special priority.

fig.note: Ferry at 30 knots · you are motoring

q: You are motoring. These lights are on your port bow on a steady bearing. Your action?
a: Hold course and speed, ready to act
o: Turn to port to pass astern of her
Turn to starboard and give way
Stop — she has the right of way
why: Rules 15 and 17: you see her green, so she has you to starboard and gives way.

q: You are the stand-on vessel and she shows no sign of giving way. What do you do first?
a: Sound at least five short blasts
o: Turn to port across her bow
Sound one prolonged blast
Keep silent and hold on
why: Rule 34(d): five short blasts when in doubt the other is taking enough action.

fig.note: Steady bearing, half a mile, no action

q: She still does nothing after your five short blasts. You decide to act. Which way?
a: Turn to starboard, not to port
o: Turn to port to pass astern of her
Speed up to cross ahead of her
Hold on — stand-on may never act
why: Rule 17(c): do not turn to port for a power vessel on your own port side.

q: She is now so close that her action alone cannot avoid a collision. What does Rule 17 require?
a: You must take the best action to avoid her
o: Hold course and speed to the end
Sound five short and do nothing else
Wait — she is the give-way vessel
why: Rule 17(b): when the give-way vessel alone cannot avoid collision, you must act.

q: Under sail, you are stand-on to this container ship. Why do you still watch her closely and act early if she does not alter?
a: She may not see you, and can't turn or stop fast
o: Ships always have the right of way over yachts
Because she is crossing from your starboard side
Ships are not allowed to alter course for yachts
why: Rules 2 and 17: big ships have blind arcs and long stopping distances.

fig.note: Open water · she is not restricted

q: You are under sail and converging with a ship showing these shapes. Who keeps clear?
a: You — she is not under command
o: She does — power gives way to sail
Whoever has the other on her port side
Neither — she is at anchor
why: Rule 18: sail keeps clear of a vessel not under command (two balls).

q: Motoring past a dredger working in the harbour approach, you see these shapes. What do you do?
a: Keep clear — she is restricted in manoeuvre
o: Hold course — she is just a power vessel
Pass close to read her signals
Keep clear only if she is to starboard
why: Rule 18: ball-diamond-ball = restricted in ability to manoeuvre.

q: Under sail, you are converging with a deep-laden tanker showing this shape. What do you do?
a: Keep out of her way — avoid impeding her
o: Hold on — she gives way to sail
Pass close ahead — she can slow down
Nothing — the shape is for fishing boats
why: Rule 18(d): all but NUC and RAM avoid impeding a vessel constrained by her draught.

q: Motoring, you see this boat crossing on a steady bearing. Who keeps clear?
a: She does — trolling is not "engaged in fishing"
o: You — fishing boats always have the priority
You — she has fishing lines in the water
Neither — both of you should slow down
why: Rule 3(d): trolling lines do not restrict manoeuvring, so Rule 15 applies.

fig.note: Trolling lines astern, no day shape

q: Under sail near Corfu, this seaplane is taxiing towards your track. Who keeps clear?
a: The seaplane — it keeps clear of vessels
o: You — aircraft always have priority
You — it is on your starboard side
Neither — it is about to take off
why: Rule 18(e): a seaplane on the water keeps well clear of all vessels.

q: You are sailing like this with the engine running in gear. What do you hoist?
a: A cone, point down, forward
o: A black ball forward
Two cones, points together
Nothing — the sails say you are sailing
why: Rule 25(e): under sail and engine, show a cone apex down; you are power-driven.

q: You are under sail alone, on port tack. This yacht on starboard tack is crossing your course. Who keeps clear?
a: She does — she is power-driven
o: You do — she is on starboard tack
Neither — both have sails up
Whichever boat is to windward
why: Rule 18: the cone shows she is motor-sailing, so she keeps clear of sail.

q: This vessel lies across your planned route into a Croatian bay. What do you do?
a: Keep well clear — she is aground in shallows
o: Pass close astern — she is only at anchor
Pass either side — she is fishing
Stand by — she is not under command
why: Rule 30(d): three balls = aground; there is shallow water round her.

q: Motoring at night, you see these lights. Where do you pass?
a: Well astern of the tow, never between
o: Close ahead of the tug, then clear
Between the tug and the lit tow
Just astern of the tug, ahead of the tow
why: Three masthead lights: a tow over 200 m long, behind the tug — never cut between.

q: Off this beach, what does good seamanship ask of you?
a: Slow down, keep well off and watch them
o: Hold course — they must keep clear
Sound five short and carry on
Speed up to get through quickly
why: Rules 2, 5 and 6: fast, unpredictable craft call for a wide berth and safe speed.

fig.title: Off a beach on Paros
lines: Your route passes 300 m off the beach

q: Motoring, you meet this windsurfer crossing ahead. Who keeps clear?
a: You — treat her as a sailing vessel
o: She does — she is far more agile
She does — she is on your port side
Neither — she is not a vessel
why: Rule 18: power keeps clear of sail; give boards a wide berth.

q: Motoring, you see this trawler crossing from your port side. Who keeps clear?
a: You — she is engaged in fishing
o: She does — you are on her starboard side
She does — she is power-driven too
Both of you alter to starboard
why: Rule 18(a): power keeps clear of a vessel engaged in fishing, from any side.

q: Motoring at night, you see only these two lights, close together, on a steady bearing. What do you do?
a: Keep clear — she is a yacht under sail
o: Hold course — she must give way to you
Turn to port across her bow
Stand on — she is only a small boat
why: No masthead light: a sailing vessel; power keeps clear of sail (Rule 18).

q: You are under sail alone and see these lights on a steady bearing. What do you do?
a: Hold course and speed, watching her closely
o: Give way — she is on your starboard side
Turn to port to pass astern of her
Tack at once to keep clear of her
why: Masthead light and red = power vessel crossing; she keeps clear of sail (Rule 18).

q: Under sail at night, you see these lights converging. Who keeps clear?
a: You — she is restricted in manoeuvre
o: She does — power gives way to sail
She does — she is on your port side
Neither — she is at anchor
why: Red-white-red all-round = restricted in ability to manoeuvre; sail keeps clear.

q: You must pass this fishing vessel. Which side do you choose?
a: The right-hand side, away from the extra white
o: The left-hand side, by the extra white
Either side — she is not making way
Close past her, whichever side is shorter
why: Rule 26(c): an extra all-round white shows the direction of outlying gear.

q: You hear this signal. What does Rule 19 require you to do?
a: Slow to steerage way, and stop if needed
o: Keep speed and sound one short blast
Turn to starboard and keep your speed
Hold course and speed — you stand on
why: Rule 19(e): a fog signal heard forward of the beam — cut to bare steerage way.

fig.title: Fog, no radar
lines: Heard: one prolonged blast every 2 min
It seems to come from your port bow

q: In fog, radar shows this target closing. Which alteration is right?
a: A bold turn to starboard, or slow down
o: A turn to port, away from the target
None — hold on as the stand-on vessel
Speed up to pass ahead of the target
why: Rule 19(d)(i): avoid turning to port for a vessel forward of the beam.

fig.note: Fog · radar only, bearing steady, closing

q: In fog, radar shows this target closing from your starboard quarter. What do you do?
a: Alter to port, away from her
o: Alter to starboard, the usual way
Hold on — she is overtaking, so she keeps clear
Turn towards her to pass under her stern
why: Rule 19(d)(ii): avoid turning towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.

fig.note: Fog · not in sight, she is faster

q: In fog, radar shows this vessel closing from your port bow. Are you the stand-on vessel?
a: No — out of sight, both must act
o: Yes — she is on your port side
No — you are the give-way vessel
Yes, until she is within a mile
why: Rule 19: vessels not in sight have no stand-on or give-way; each avoids close quarters.

fig.note: Fog · not in sight of each other

q: You were tracking this motor yacht by radar in fog. Now she is in sight. Which rule applies?
a: The crossing rule — you give way to her
o: Still Rule 19 — nobody is stand-on
You stand on — she is the faster boat
Both of you turn to port to open up
why: Rules 11 and 15: once in sight of each other, the steering rules apply.

fig.note: She has just come into sight, 200 m off

q: Motoring at 5 knots in fog, what sound signal do you make?
a: One prolonged blast every 2 minutes or less
o: Two prolonged blasts every 2 minutes
One prolonged and two short every 2 minutes
Five short blasts every minute
why: Rule 35(a): power-driven, making way — one prolonged at intervals of 2 minutes or less.

q: Fog closes in while you are under sail alone. Which signal do you give, and how often?
a: One prolonged and two short, every 2 minutes
o: One prolonged, every 2 minutes
Two prolonged, every 2 minutes
Rapid ringing of the bell, every minute
why: Rule 35(c): a sailing vessel sounds one prolonged followed by two short.

q: In thick fog you stop the engine and drift, sails furled, to listen. What signal now?
a: Two prolonged blasts every 2 minutes or less
o: One prolonged blast every 2 minutes or less
One prolonged, two short, every 2 minutes
None — you are not making way through the water
why: Rule 35(b): under way but not making way — two prolonged blasts.

q: In fog you hear three separate strokes of a bell, rapid ringing, then three strokes again, ahead of you. What do you do?
a: Keep well clear — a vessel aground, shoal water
o: Pass close — it is just a vessel at anchor
Hold on — a vessel under way must give way
Ignore it — it is a church bell ashore
why: Rule 35(h): three strokes, rapid ringing, three strokes = vessel aground.

q: Motoring slowly along the coast in fog, you hear rapid ringing of a bell for about five seconds, once a minute. What is it?
a: A boat at anchor — slow down and avoid her
o: A vessel aground — the water is shallow
A sailing vessel under way
A fishing boat hauling her nets
why: Rule 35(g): rapid bell ringing for 5 seconds each minute = vessel at anchor.

q: Creeping into a bay in fog, you hear one short, one prolonged and one short blast close ahead. What does it mean?
a: An anchored boat warns you are closing on her
o: A vessel aground somewhere ahead of you
A ship astern intending to overtake you
A sailing vessel under way close by
why: Rule 35(g): an anchored vessel may sound short-prolonged-short as a warning.

q: A motor yacht you can see clearly sounds two short blasts. What is she doing?
a: Altering her course to port
o: Altering her course to starboard
Going astern
Asking you to keep clear
why: Rule 34(a): two short = I am altering my course to port.

q: In a busy island harbour, a ferry near the quay sounds three short blasts. What does it mean?
a: Her engines are going astern
o: She is altering course to starboard
She doubts what you are doing
She is about to leave — clear the way
why: Rule 34(a): three short = I am operating astern propulsion.

q: You are near a ship in clear weather when she sounds five short, rapid blasts. What does she mean?
a: She doubts you are keeping clear
o: She is altering course to port
She is going astern
She is about to overtake you
why: Rule 34(d): at least five short = I doubt your intentions or action.

q: Motoring in sight of this ship, you are about to alter to starboard to give way. What signal do you give?
a: One short blast as you turn
o: Two short blasts as you turn
One prolonged blast
None — signals are for ships only
why: Rule 34(a): power vessels in sight signal alterations — one short = to starboard.

q: You have not yet altered for this ship. She flashes a white light five times, rapidly. What does she mean?
a: She doubts you are keeping clear — act now
o: She is altering her course to port
She is turning to starboard to avoid you
She wants you to hold course and speed
why: Rule 34(d): five short, rapid flashes = doubt; give way clearly now.

q: This ship flashes her all-round white light twice. What is she doing?
a: Altering her course to port
o: Altering her course to starboard
Operating astern propulsion
Warning you of danger ahead
why: Rule 34(b): two flashes, like two short blasts = altering to port.

q: There is no room to turn to starboard for this motorboat. What do you do?
a: Slow down or stop until she has passed
o: Turn to starboard anyway — Rule 14
Turn to port and pass starboard to starboard
Hold course and speed — she will move
why: Rules 2(b) and 8(e): when the rule cannot be followed, slow or stop.
